paragraphs.text: Waldemar Tomaszewski (ECR), raštuPonia Pirmininke,Diskusijos dėl ES krizių plano kalbant apie sveikatos priežiūros darbuotojus yra būtinas ir esminis atsakas į blogėjančias sveikatos priežiūros sektoriuje dirbančių žmonių darbo sąlygas ir atlyginimus. Tai ypač svarbu kalbant apie vidutinio lygio darbuotojus. Sveikatos priežiūros darbuotojų trūkumas yra vienas iš svarbiausių strateginių iššūkių Europos Sąjungos valstybių narių sveikatos priežiūros sistemų atsparumui ir kokybei. Turimi duomenys šia tema kelia nerimą. ES šalyse pranešama, kad trūksta apie apie 1,2 milijono gydytojų, slaugytojų ir akušerių, reikalingų užtikrinti visuotinę prieigą prie sveikatos priežiūros paslaugų.Be to, sveikatos priežiūros darbuotojų ir personalo sektoriaus krizę dar labiau pagilina tai, kad pensinio amžiaus grupės, palyginti su šiuo metu mažėjančiu su sveikata susijusias studijas pasirenkančių studentų skaičiumi ir naujų absolventų srautu, rodo, kad ateityje sveikatos priežiūros darbo jėgos atotrūkis didės. Dėl šios priežasties, siekiant geriau apsaugoti mūsų piliečių sveikatą, reikia imtis visapusiškų veiksmų – nuo paskatų studijuoti medicinos sritis iki medicinos personalo atlyginimų didinimo. Be konkrečių finansinių paskatų sunku bus užpildyti dabartinį darbuotojų trūkumą. Sveikatos priežiūros darbuotojų krizė kelia rimtą viešąjį iššūkį, kuriam reikia teikti pirmenybę. Nepamirškime, kad pakankamas personalo lygis, geros darbo sąlygos ir tinkama sveikatos priežiūros darbuotojų sudėtis yra būtini pacientų saugumui.

paragraphs.text: L'ordine del giorno reca la discussione sull'interrogazione con richiesta di risposta orale alla Commissione sul rafforzamento della resilienza sanitaria globale nei paesi partner, di Barry Andrews, a nome della commissione per lo sviluppo (O-000033/2026 - B10-0015/2026) (2026/2731(RSP)).

interventions.text: L'ordine del giorno reca la discussione sull'interrogazione con richiesta di risposta orale alla Commissione sul rafforzamento della resilienza sanitaria globale nei paesi partner, di Barry Andrews, a nome della commissione per lo sviluppo (O-000033/2026 - B10-0015/2026) (2026/2731(RSP)).

paragraphs.text: Madam President, Commissioner Síkela and colleagues, it's great that we're having this debate on an ambitious global health policy. We do global health because it's the right thing to do. We do global health because there have been extraordinary gains in, for example, child mortality in the last decades. So it works. It actually works. And that's why it's important that we resurface the assumptions behind this policy during the course of this short debate.

It is the right thing to do, but there are secondary consequences. It also helps to deliver European security. It also helps to ensure the prosperity of the European economy. There is widespread evidence that official development assistance delivers for the European economy, it delivers for EU exports, it opens up markets and trade routes that might not otherwise have worked. So not only does it deliver for the beneficiaries of an ambitious global health policy, but it delivers for Europe as well.

So if we're changing that, we better know exactly what we're doing. If we decide that we're going to move away from that model, we have to be very careful about it. And unfortunately, of course, in 2025, there were dramatic cuts in aid, a reduction of 25 % over 2024. This is a cliff edge and the consequences are already being felt. There are fewer girls going to school today in 2026 than there were two years ago. There are more cases of child marriage than there were two years ago. There are more cases of cholera. There's more cases of transmission of childhood HIV and AIDS. So the situation is urgent.

There has been a lot of effort made to try to manage this transition by primary health care, as in by health institutions across the world. That is true. But the problem is that the coping mechanism has been shifting away from long-term interventions, shifting away from prevention into immediate emergency issues. So that has masked the overall impact of the numbers. But that's not something that can be masked forever. The current outbreak of Ebola in DRC is a good example of things that are working. It is contained. We have learned some of the lessons from the outbreak in West Africa in 2014 and 2015, but there are some lessons that we did not learn.

So there are two main points that I want to make about the global lessons that have to be adopted. First of all, the World Health Organisation is at the centre of the global health architecture, the World Health Assembly and the WHO guidelines. And we have to, as the European Union, really promote this multilateralism. We have to have early warning systems, we have to have surveillance. We have to encourage public institutions to declare a pandemic at the earliest possible opportunity. And we have to discourage the private sector from withdrawing from places where pandemics take place, because that, of course, disincentivises public authorities from reporting honestly.

Secondly, we have to invest in health system strengthening. This is one of the key lessons from the outbreak in West Africa in 2015. To give one example, in Sierra Leone today, there is one doctor for every 10 000 head of population. By contrast, in my country, Ireland, we have 40 doctors per 10 000 head of population. Now, it's a slight improvement in Sierra Leone, actually, from where it was in 2014. But it just goes to show that this is the core issue. If we really are serious about avoiding the next pandemic, which would have a devastating effect on the European economy, wiping out all of the competitiveness gains that we've worked so diligently to achieve, then we must invest in global health and health system strengthening in particular. And I mean the Africa CDC, I mean in cooperation in Horizon with African universities, I mean in vaccines and therapeutics and diagnostics. Africa imports 99 % of its vaccines, it imports 90 % of its medicines and there's lots of work to do.

I just want to make a final point about Global Gateway. Less than 10 % of Global Gateway projects are actually invested in health. So the reality is a little bit different to how it's presented. Less than 10 % of Global Gateway projects. So Parliament will endeavour to scrutinise properly these health flagships in the years to come. We're going to really look closely at not only the inputs, the leverage of private sector investment and whether it can actually reach fragile states, but also the overall impact. And that's our job, and that's something we will do. We will also try and shift the emphasis away from infrastructure and manufacturing, which is good, onto primary healthcare and health system strengthening. I think that balance has to be achieved. And finally, we also have to focus on fragile states. Unfortunately, many fragile states are not bankable. They're not investable. They don't have the governance, compliance and regulatory environment that Global Gateway thrives in. And so we have to keep that in mind. So finally, I repeat, we have to have a global health policy that is ambitious and reflects both knowing the right thing to do as well as doing it in our own interests as well.

interventions.speaker_label: Jozef Síkela, Member of the Commission.

paragraphs.text: Madam President, honourable Members, as global challenges intensify, the pressure on global health continues to mount: conflicts, forced displacement, climate disasters, disease outbreaks and disinformation campaigns. Each one of these challenges takes a toll on the health and well-being of people around the world. Take, for example, the deadly Ebola outbreak, worsened by the conflict in the DRC. These challenges occur against a backdrop of declining global health funds and rising politicisation of health investment.

In May, the Commission adopted the global health resilience initiative. This is not about creating another health programme. This is about uniting Europe's investments and expertise behind a common goal, delivering greater impact where it is needed most, while supporting EU strategic autonomy and competitiveness. We do this through nine flagship initiatives that boost health at local, national and regional and global levels.

Together with a broad range of stakeholders, we are supporting country-led health systems, from strengthening primary care to increasing access for vulnerable populations, including women and girls. Boosting countries' capacity and creating an environment conducive to producing medicines and vaccines through Global Gateway. Detecting health threats faster, and strengthening prevention, preparedness and response capacity. Countering disinformation through evidence-based communication and greater access to scientific research. Providing lifesaving healthcare to those in fragile settings through humanitarian assistance. And strengthening cooperation between governments, civil society and multilateral organisations.

Next week, in the margins of UNGA, I will host a side event bringing together key partners in global health architecture, including the World Health Organization and other UN bodies, governments and the private sector to discuss our shared challenges.

Honourable Members, I am pleased that your resolution closely aligns with our approach to global health. We have a unique opportunity to build a more coherent, country-owned and equitable global health architecture that supports our partners in their transition to health sovereignty. Through more effective coordination, financing and collaboration, we can really maximise our impact.

paragraphs.text: Madam President, Commissioner, it is highly appreciated that, given your busy schedule – and I know about your busy schedule very well – you are always present in the European Parliament when your issues are discussed, and this is of utmost importance for our parliamentary endeavour here at European level. I also thank Barry Andrews, our DEVE Chair, for his initiative to make this motion for a resolution on global health.

First and foremost, I want to share my clear view that global health investments from Europe's side is not a gift to anybody, but it is an investment in Europe's health, in Europe's stability and in the resilience of Europeans when it comes to health, because health issues don't know borders at all. We knew that before the pandemic, we had proof of that due to the pandemic and during the pandemic, and we see today that we have to invest in other parts of the world – especially, of course, in the capability of these other parts of the world themselves to invest in health.
How people treat each other when it comes to preparedness for health issues, when it comes to treatment in health issues and when it comes to diseases says a lot about societies.
So how we deal in health crises says a lot also about how we conduct the principles of human dignity, of individual freedom, and of each person being worth the same.
This is what we spread as Europe, not only in terms of money, but also in terms of good example, and it means a lot to the world.

political_group.label: PPE
political_group.name: Group of the European People's Party (Christian Democrats)

interventions.speaker_label: Christophe Clergeau, au nom du groupe S&D.

paragraphs.text: Madame la Présidente, Monsieur le Commissaire, je voudrais d'abord remercier notre collègue Barry Andrews d'avoir pris l'initiative de ce débat, dire que je partage son propos et que ce qui est en cause, c'est bien la santé globale des populations sur la planète et la sécurité de l'Europe et la santé des Européens.

Et il y a urgence, Monsieur le Commissaire. La communication de la Commission et ce que vous avez décrit comme initiative, c'est positif, mais les effets seront des effets de moyen-terme. L'urgence est absolue, elle est là, elle est liée au retrait américain. On voit partout, en Afrique et dans le reste du monde, reculer les actions de prévention et les actions de mobilisation de vaccination, reculer la lutte contre le sida. On voit avec Ebola la fragilisation des systèmes de santé; dans certains pays, ce sont des dizaines de milliers de personnes qui ont été licenciées.

Donc moi, la question que je pose est très simple: c'est comment l'Europe et l'Organisation mondiale de la santé sécurisent la santé mondiale en assurant la pérennité des systèmes de santé et des actions de prévention partout? Et je voudrais que vous nous disiez quel est le budget qui va être mobilisé, d'où qu'il vienne: L’Europe dans le monde, le Mécanisme européen de protection civile, HERA ou le programme «L'UE pour la santé» pour réellement être aux côtés de nos partenaires du reste du monde et éviter l'effondrement de la santé mondiale et la mise en danger également de la santé des Européens.

political_group.name: Group of the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats in the European Parliament

interventions.speaker_label: Gerald Hauser, im Namen der PfE-Fraktion.

paragraphs.text: Frau Präsidentin! Es ist recht interessant, Herr Kommissar. Wir haben gerade vorhin über die Probleme des Gesundheitswesens in der Europäischen Union diskutiert: Es fehlen 4,1 Millionen Fachkräfte im Gesundheitsbereich. Und jetzt diskutieren wir: „Was können wir tun, um in Partnerländern das Gesundheitswesen zu stärken?“ Also hochinteressant, wo Schwerpunkte gesetzt werden.

Zur angesprochenen Desinformation auch ein Beispiel: Herr Kommissar und Kollegen, Sie wissen ja, während der sogenannten Pandemie wurde uns mitgeteilt von Ihnen, dass es wichtig ist, Kinder zu impfen; mit dem Argument: Kinder müssen deswegen geimpft werden, damit sie den COVID‑Virus nicht übertragen können, damit sie ihre Großeltern besuchen können. So war es doch! Und wir haben uns immer gegen Kinderimpfungen ausgesprochen und wurden dann als Schwurbler und Verbreiter von Desinformation bezeichnet. Ich zitiere jetzt, ich zitiere jetzt eine parlamentarische Anfrage, beantwortet von Gesundheitskommissar Várhelyi, genau diese Impfung betreffend, aktuell am 24. August bekommen. Ich zitiere: „Die Indikation, für die die Impfstoffe zugelassen wurden, war die Prävention schwerer Erkrankungen durch die Infektion und nicht speziell die Prävention einer Virusübertragung.“ Das heißt, Sie wussten, dass mit der COVID-Impfung die Menschen nicht geschützt werden, Kinder nicht geschützt werden, das Virus zu übertragen – das wussten Sie! Und trotzdem haben Sie die Eltern aufgefordert, die Kinder zu impfen. Ich frage Sie: Wer hat damals Desinformation verbreitet? Waren Sie das? Wir waren es nicht!

interventions.speaker_label: Małgorzata Gosiewska, w imieniu grupy ECR.

paragraphs.text: Pani Przewodnicząca! Szanowni Państwo! Wzmacnianie odporności zdrowotnej państw partnerskich nie może oznaczać jedynie przekazywania kolejnych pieniędzy z Europy. Pomoc musi odpowiadać na rzeczywiste potrzeby ludzi i wzmacniać samodzielność. Mieszkańcy Afryki potrzebują trwałych systemów, szpitali, diagnostyki, personelu medycznego i realnego dostępu do leczenia.

Zamiast pompować kolejne środki w pojedyncze, prywatne przedsięwzięcia, powinniśmy wspierać tworzenie systemów ubezpieczeń zdrowotnych, które pozwolą leczyć także najuboższych, a może przede wszystkim najuboższych. Unia może je czasowo współfinansować, a dalsze wsparcie powinno zależeć od ich skuteczności, przejrzystości i podejmowania odpowiedzialności przez państwo partnerskie.

Nie możemy też akceptować sytuacji, w której pod hasłem pomocy zdrowotnej narzuca się państwom partnerskim rozwiązania ideologiczne, w tym promowanie aborcji, zamiast koncentrować się na zdrowiu matek, kobiet, dzieci.

Pomoc ma budować samodzielność, a nie – zależność. Samodzielna i bardziej sprawna Afryka to bardziej bezpieczna Europa. Dziękuję przewodniczącemu Komisji, za podjęcie tego tematu, ale dziękuję też, panie komisarzu, za zaangażowanie w przygotowywanie zmian systemowych. Na nie liczymy.

interventions.speaker_label: Erik Marquardt, im Namen der Verts/ALE-Fraktion.

paragraphs.text: Frau Präsidentin! Herr Kommissar, schön, dass Sie da sind. Die globale Gesundheitsfinanzierung wurde in den vergangenen Jahren um mehr als 50 % gekürzt. Man kann nun einerseits sich Tabellen angucken und sagen, „Mensch, das ist ja weniger Geld“, aber ich glaube, wir tun gut daran, uns ganz konkret anzuschauen, was das für Menschenleben bedeutet, was das für Menschen bedeutet.

Es gibt eine Studie von The Lancet, die besagt, dass bis 2030 bei diesen Kürzungen 22,6 Millionen Menschen zusätzlich sterben könnten. Und natürlich kann man sich jetzt fragen – machen ja manche auf der rechten Seite dann –, was geht uns das eigentlich an; sie sind ja nicht in Europa; ist uns ja irgendwie egal, dass die Menschen sterben.

Aber ich möchte eigentlich, dass wir uns schon auch in Europa darauf einigen, dass es am Ende doch nicht sein kann, dass wir laut dieser Studie dann zum Beispiel 5,4 Millionen Kindern unter fünf Jahren sagen, dass wir leider andere Prioritäten haben, als dafür zu sorgen, dass sie eine Zukunft haben. Ich glaube, diese ethische und moralische Ebene ist wichtig, aber es ist natürlich auch wichtig, dass wir ein eigenes Interesse daran haben, dass es der Welt besser geht.

Es geht ja nicht nur um Gesundheit von Menschen, es geht auch um Gesundheit von politischen Systemen; es geht um Krisenprävention, Vorsorge; es geht darum, dass wir zum Beispiel so eine globale Pandemie, wie wir sie gerade erlebt haben, nicht noch einmal erleben. Und dafür ist es natürlich wichtig, dass wir uns damit beschäftigen.
Es wäre schön, wenn hier auch 27 Staats- und Regierungschefs sitzen würden, die in ihren Haushalten dann dafür den Weg freimachen, aber daran arbeiten wir. Ich bedanke mich erstmal für diese Debatte.

interventions.speaker_role_in_transcript: em nome do Grupo The Left

paragraphs.text: Senhora Presidente, eu queria agradecer a oportunidade desta pergunta oral. Há aqui alguns debates absurdos no Parlamento. Eu gostava de tentar explicar muito brevemente porque é que não há nenhuma oposição entre prioridade à resposta na saúde na Europa e prioridade à saúde global. Porque qualquer pessoa com dois dedos de testa sabe que, se não houvesse cooperação global, a Covid-19 tinha sido uma desgraça ainda maior. Porque qualquer pessoa com dois dedos de testa sabe que, sem cooperação global, nós não tínhamos um surto de ébola nalguns sítios em África — tínhamos também na Europa.

É por isso que não há nenhuma escolha entre uma coisa ou outra. Mas há uma escolha, sim, que temos de fazer: em quem confiamos para dar resposta de saúde global. E nós sabemos que o setor privado da saúde não esteve lá durante a Covid-19, como não está lá nos surtos de ébola. Nós sabemos que as patentes e a propriedade intelectual têm, aliás, sido um obstáculo muitas vezes aos tratamentos fundamentais às pessoas. E é por isso que acharmos que parcerias público-privadas na saúde global vão resolver o problema é um erro.

Precisamos de investimento público e de investimento público certo. E precisamos de apoiar os serviços de saúde locais e que haja profissionais em todos os locais. Isso é fundamental. E, no mundo de Trump, o mínimo que se exige à União Europeia é que seja a sensata nesta sala. Porque, se nós desprotegermos a cooperação mundial em saúde, se nós esquecermos os direitos globais, não há nenhuma fronteira, não há nenhuma arma que vá proteger a saúde e a vida dos europeus.

interventions.speaker_label: Marc Jongen, im Namen der ESN-Fraktion.

paragraphs.text: Frau Präsidentin! Meine Damen und Herren! Herr Kommissar Síkela! Nach Corona hat die Europäische Union in der Gesundheitspolitik sehr viel Vertrauen verspielt − und die WHO erst recht! Sie weigert sich bis heute, ihre Fehler einzugestehen, geschweige denn, sie aufzuklären. Und ausgerechnet diese Akteure wollen uns jetzt eine globale Gesundheitsstrategie verkaufen.

6 Milliarden EUR hat die EU von 2021 bis 2025 für globale Gesundheit ausgegeben. 22 % des WHO-Haushalts kommen aus der Union, den Löwenanteil zahlt wie immer Deutschland. Wir sind der größte Geldgeber einer Organisation, die Lockdowns, Impfzwang und Zensur mitgetragen hat und für die allen Ernstes ein Karl Lauterbach als Direktor im Gespräch ist, der während Corona kläglich versagt hat.

Man hat ja − wie immer − nur die besten Absichten. Was aber die Kommission Resilienz nennt, das ist der Ausbau eines latent totalitären Gesundheitsregimes. Stärkere Koordination multilateraler Strukturen – das heißt mehr Macht für die WHO! Vertrauen in die Wissenschaft und der Kampf gegen tatsächliche oder angebliche Desinformation – das bedeutet, abweichende Meinungen, und zwar auch fachlich fundierte zur Wirksamkeit von Impfungen, sollen unterdrückt werden. DSA-Faktenchecker und Democracy Shield lassen grüßen.

Herr Kommissar Síkela, drei Fragen. Erstens: Wie wollen Sie verhindern, dass aus globaler Gesundheitsresilienz wieder die totalitäre Kontrolle der Bürger wird, die wir unter Corona erlebt haben – Überwachung, Reiseverbote, Berufsverbote, soziale Ächtung? Zweitens: Wer definiert Desinformation? Die Kommission, die WHO, bezahlte Faktenchecker? Und drittens: Wird die Kommission eine unabhängige Untersuchung der WHO-Pandemiepolitik unterstützen oder weiter Geld nach Genf überweisen und so tun, als sei nichts gewesen? Die ESN-Fraktion lehnt jede Aufstockung der EU-Mittel für die WHO, die Bill Gates als größten privaten Spender hat, entschieden ab. Sogar Angela Merkel hat ja inzwischen zugegeben, welchen Impfdruck die Gates-Stiftung in der Coronazeit auf Regierungen weltweit ausgeübt hat.

Einige Punkte gehen auch in die richtige Richtung. Medikamente müssen wieder dort hergestellt werden, wo man sie braucht, in den Partnerländern und in Europa selbst. Es braucht keine Pandemie, um zu verstehen: Wir dürfen uns bei der Gesundheit nicht von China abhängig machen. Problematisch ist aber eben die ideologische Ladung, die Kommission und Ausschuss in die Entschließung hineingeschrieben haben. Sexuelle und reproduktive Gesundheit und Rechte heißt in der Praxis: EU-Geld und Propaganda für Abtreibungen. Angebracht wäre Schutz der Mütter und Kampf gegen Kindersterblichkeit. Dazu kommt die Genderideologie − LGBTQ als Pflichtprogramm für Partnerländer, deren Kulturen und Rechtsordnungen das mehrheitlich ablehnen.

Wir brauchen keinen solchen neokolonialen Export westlicher linker Identitätspolitik, sondern kosteneffiziente Prävention in den Partnerländern, dort wo es nötig ist. Kein neues Fass ohne Boden, keine ideologische Agenda und kein Zensur- und Überwachungsregime im Namen der Gesundheit!

interventions.speaker_label: Jozef Síkela, Member of the Commission.

paragraphs.text: Madam President, honourable Members, thank you for your insights and recommendations. I will keep them in mind and we will continue to roll out the global health resilience initiative. I also want to thank Barry Andrews for initiating this debate.
Maybe a short answer to your question. How? Very simple: evidence-based.
Let me emphasise a few points.

Going forward, the Commission remains committed to partnering fully with Member States to maximise impacts. From 2021 to 2025, the EU mobilised, as already mentioned, over EUR 6 billion to build global health resilience. Together with the World Health Organization, we are supporting stronger health systems in 115 countries across Africa, the Caribbean, Latin America, Asia, the MENA region and Europe. Through Global Gateway, we mobilised more than EUR 2 billion for regional manufacturing of vaccines and medicines. Today, production sites are taking shape in Senegal, Ghana, Nigeria, Rwanda and South Africa, and we are bringing together researchers, universities, regulators and health professionals to build self-sustaining ecosystems. In times of crisis, the EU steps up humanitarian assistance and response.
As for the Ebola outbreak, with over EUR 200 million in immediate humanitarian aid, surveillance and research funding.

While some global actors may retreat from their commitments, we are fully engaged to deliver better health outcomes for people. The EU stands ready to do its part as a reliable partner at the global, regional and country levels.

paragraphs.text: Poštovana predsjedavajuća, povjereniče, kolegice i kolege, zdravstvene prijetnje ne poznaju granice.

Upravo zato Europa mora biti spremna zaštititi svoje građane, pravodobno prepoznati rizike i spriječiti da zdravstvene krize prerastu prekogranične prijetnje. Prevencija mora biti naš prioritet. Rano otkrivanje bolesti, učinkoviti sustavi upozoravanja, razmjena relevantnih podataka i bolja pripravnost mogu spriječiti širenje epidemije i smanjiti njihove zdravstvene, društvene i gospodarske posljedice.

Istodobno, dugoročno jačanje zdravstvenih sustava partnerskih država mora se temeljiti na odgovornosti njih samih. Oni moraju graditi snažne institucije, ulagati u vlastite zdravstvene radnike i osiguravati održivo financiranje svojih zdravstvenih sustava mobilizacijom vlastitih resursa. Europska unija, naravno, pritom može i treba biti pouzdan partner. Naša suradnja treba jačati njihove kapacitete, a ne stvarati trajnu ovisnost. Zato europska razvojna politika mora biti usmjerena na konkretne potrebe, jasne ciljeve, mjerljive rezultate i dugoročnu održivost. Jednako je važna bolja koordinacija između Europske unije, država članica, partnerskih zemalja i međunarodnih organizacija. Moramo smanjiti fragmentaciju i preklapanje programa te osigurati učinkovitije korištenje raspoloživih sredstava. Naš je cilj jasan: spriječiti zdravstvene prijetnje prije nego što prijeđu granice, ojačati pripravnost Europe i pomoći partnerskim zemljama da izgrade snažne i održive vlastite kapacitete.

Kolegice i kolege, partnerstvo mora počivati na uzajamnoj odgovornosti. Europa će ostati pouzdan partner, ali trajna otpornost trećih država može se izgraditi samo tamo gdje država preuzima odgovornost za vlastite zdravstvene sustave.

paragraphs.text: Señora presidenta, señor comisario, en el 2020 vimos cómo un virus detectado en un lugar concreto del mundo ponía en jaque nuestra seguridad y nuestra sociedad, paraba nuestras vidas en todo el mundo en muy pocos días.

Es verdad que tuvimos una cooperación científica sin precedentes y conseguimos unas vacunas en tiempo récord. Pero cometimos un grave error: aprovisionar el 87 % de las vacunas en los países del norte y solo el 0,2 % fue distribuido en los países de renta a baja. En los países de renta media de América Latina la mortalidad fue devastadora.
Aquello no fue solo una injusticia, fue un error de seguridad sanitaria global. Porque la pandemia nos recordó algo muy sencillo: la salud es un bien global y, por eso, tenemos que tomarlo como tal.

Por eso, queremos acoger y valorar que la Comisión incluyera la salud global en sus prioridades este año a través de esta comunicación y queremos agradecerle al presidente de la Comisión de Desarrollo esta iniciativa.

Pero, ojo, la mayoría de los problemas vienen en países olvidados y debemos focalizarnos ahí: fortalecer los sistemas sanitarios, fortalecer las capacidades de prevención y respuesta de fabricación de vacunas y entender de una vez por todas que la salud global es una cuestión de solidaridad, pero también de seguridad para Europa.

paragraphs.text: Signora Presidente, signor Commissario, onorevoli colleghi, le crisi sanitarie non conoscono confini e rafforzare i sistemi sanitari dei Paesi partner significa proteggere anche la salute e la sicurezza dell'Europa.

Il Piano Mattei indica una strada che può diventare un modello europeo: partenariati paritari e investimenti costruiti sulle reali esigenze dei territori. Di fronte a sfide come la resistenza antimicrobica, le pandemie e i farmaci falsificati, dobbiamo continuare a contrastare HIV, tubercolosi e malaria; ma dobbiamo, soprattutto, rafforzare le capacità locali.

Questo significa investire nella telemedicina, collegare i territori alle reti di specialisti europei e trasferire conoscenze e competenze. Significa, anche promuovere cofinanziamenti e partnership tra imprese europee e produttori locali, favorendo il trasferimento tecnologico e la creazione di hub produttivi, sempre nel quadro di una solida governance pubblica.
Perché investire nella salute non significa, soltanto, garantire cure migliori: significa creare crescita, stabilità e maggiore sicurezza per i Paesi partner e, soprattutto, per l'Europa.

paragraphs.text: Señora presidenta, señor comisario, la pandemia nos enseñó que la resiliencia sanitaria no se construye cuando llega la crisis, sino que se tiene que construir desde mucho antes.

La política de salud mundial debe ser una prioridad estratégica para la Unión Europea no solamente por solidaridad, sino también por seguridad mundial. En un momento de creciente inestabilidad geográfica, y también de recortes en la financiación de la salud pública mundial, Europa tiene que dar un paso al frente: apostar por reforzar la resiliencia sanitaria mundial es clave.

Debemos asegurarnos de que la cooperación genere capacidades —y no dependencia— para que sea un sistema accesible e inclusivo. Para esto, tenemos que dedicar especial atención a todos los colectivos vulnerables, especialmente a las niñas, las mujeres y las personas con discapacidad. Es también muy importante contrarrestar la desinformación sanitaria y garantizar políticas de vacunación eficaces.

Y por último, la ambición de la Unión Europea para poder ejercer este liderazgo en materia de salud mundial tiene que ir acompañada de financiación suficiente. Y por esto pedimos qué partidas presupuestarias habrá en el futuro marco financiero plurianual.

paragraphs.text: Madam President, Commissioner, colleagues, we talk about international cooperation in terms of projected growth, fiscal health and even bankability and return on investment, as if generating more money is the end goal and not the means to improve the lives of people. Growth figures can rise while inequality deepens and basic services stay out of reach. Official development aid cuts to health have amounted to EUR 5 to 7 billion in the last years, and it is putting investment in health back to the levels of 2008, hitting especially those in regions where support for accessibility of healthcare is the most needed.

We can build all the railways and ports and airports that we want, but without access to human basic needs for regular people, those investments benefit only the few. Sustainable development is about people. We need to invest in people, in their health and not just in profit.

paragraphs.text: Frau Präsidentin! Herr Kommissar! Liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen! Spätestens seit der COVID‑Pandemie wissen wir: Gesundheit kennt keine Grenzen. Gleichzeitig ist die internationale Gesundheitsfinanzierung allein von 2024 auf 2025 um 21 % eingebrochen. Ebola und andere Ausbrüche zeigen uns, welche Folgen schwache Gesundheitssysteme haben können − vor Ort, aber auch für uns in Europa.

Deshalb ist es richtig, dass Europa seine Partnerschaften stärkt. Dabei geht es aber nicht allein um finanzielle Hilfe. Europas Stärke sind Forschung, medizinische Expertise und innovative Unternehmen. Gemeinsam mit unseren Partnern müssen wir klinische Forschung ermöglichen, Wissen teilen und nachhaltige Produktionskapazitäten vor Ort aufbauen. Das stärkt Gesundheitssysteme vor Ort, diversifiziert Lieferketten für uns und eröffnet zugleich Chancen für europäische Forschung und Unternehmen. Globale Gesundheitsresilienz ist deshalb nicht nur Solidarität, sie liegt auch in unserem eigenen europäischen Interesse.

paragraphs.text: Madame la Présidente, Monsieur le Commissaire, chers collègues, la santé est un droit fondamental humain. Jamais il ne devrait dépendre du lieu de naissance, des moyens ou du genre. Pourtant, des millions de personnes n'ont toujours pas accès aux mêmes soins. Les femmes et les filles en payent particulièrement le prix. Elles sont trop souvent moins écoutées, moins prises au sérieux, moins bien diagnostiquées. L'épidémie d'Ebola en RDC le montre.

Premières à donner les soins, ce sont les femmes qui sont les plus touchées. Elles sont aussi les premières touchées par les réductions de l'aide au développement qui se multiplient. Je le regrette vivement, car ces fonds contribuent à sauver des millions de vies. Il faut inverser cette tendance pour tenir un engagement qui honore l'Union européenne: celui d'une santé véritablement universelle.

I'd like to thank my good colleague Barry Andrews for raising important questions regarding the Commission's initiative.

The pandemic proved that global health affects us all, and we cannot be resilient until healthcare systems around the world are resilient. Persistent health inequalities make people less capable of preventing and overcoming crises. That is why this initiative cannot be assessed in isolation.

Global health succeeds or fails, depending on whether we recognise its independence, with sustainable development goals. Yet, as budgets for global health shrink, Europe must reconfirm its commitment to these goals through sustained long-term funding and genuine commitment to collaboration with partner countries.

paragraphs.text: Madam President, I say to the Commissioner, when you put together vaccines with profits, you open the Pandora's box, and this Pandora's box was opened in Europe during the COVID-19 pandemic crisis.

You claim that when we talk about vaccines, we need to base our decisions on evidence. I remind you that, in this plenary, your predecessors stated that we need to approve these vaccines. I voted against those provisions, but they have to be approved in order to stop the transmission of the virus. But when the representative of Pfizer was asked if they ever tested the Pfizer vaccines, the person stated, and I quote, 'we had to move at the speed of science and we did not do it'. So it's important to look back at what happened during the pandemic, and it's sad that you turn your back to me because you have to provide concrete answers to the Europeans. paragraphs.text: Señora presidenta, señor comisario, toda crisis, también la sanitaria, nos desafía en nuestros cimientos, en lo que más apreciamos, hasta en nuestra identidad. Y es probable que salgamos peores de una crisis; pero la disciplina consiste en hacer cuanto esté en nuestra mano para ser mejores.

La COVID-19 fue un ejemplo: la Unión Europea invirtió, lo hizo conjuntamente. La Unión Europea promovió la investigación científica y técnica y colaboró con la industria en la generación de vacunas. Pero se ha puesto de manifiesto el error de su distribución desigualitaria, lo que contradice la vocación de la Unión Europea de ser primera en la fila de la ayuda humanitaria y la cooperación al desarrollo de manera equitativa y de ser globalmente relevante.

Por tanto, ahora la lección es que la Unión Europea tiene que imponer su legislación europea, no solamente para asegurar la transparencia en la distribución de las vacunas y, por tanto, combatir cualquier asomo de corrupción o de malversación de fondos a su propósito; también tiene que asegurar que la industria farmacéutica y las industrias médicas no imponen su voluntad por encima del legislador europeo.

paragraphs.text: Arvoisa puhemies, EU ei voi olla ilmainen terveyskeskus koko maailmalle. Mutta mitäpä te olette taas vaatimassa?

Euroopan eduskunnan nimissä halutaan nyt linjata, että EU:lta tarvitaan poliittisia ja taloudellisia sitoumuksia suojella globaalia terveyttä yleismaailmallisena oikeutena ja globaalina julkishyödykkeenä.

En tiedä missä utopiassa te elätte, mutta todellisessa maailmassa meillä ei riitä tähän rahat alkuunkaan. Jäsenmaat tekevät hartiavoimin töitä, että terveyspalvelut säilyisivät julkishyödykkeenä edes omille kansalaisilleen.

Tässä samassa tekstissä te kauhistelette myös kehitysavun leikkauksia. Sillä on syynsä, miksi esimerkiksi Suomen hallitus on leikannut kehitysapua. Vuosikymmenten kehitysapu on ollut äärimmäisen tehotonta, ja se on ruokkinut jo entisestään rehottavaa korruptiota. Siksi on aika sulkea kehitysavun rahahanat.

paragraphs.text: Good morning, dear colleagues. Today we welcome once again Prime Minister of Canada, Mark Carney, to this Hemicycle to speak to us directly. Dear Mark, thank you for being here.

The friendship between the European Union and Canada is rooted in our shared values and in our outlook. It is built on the same understanding that united Canadians in 1867 and Europeans in 1951: that we are always stronger when we work together. Our partnership and yours are grounded in the stories of our peoples.

Many of those who helped to build your nation were Europeans in search of a better life, and in our continent's darkest moments, Canadians were there for us. In 1914, when war shattered our continent, Canadians fought shoulder to shoulder with us through the muddy trenches of Ypres, the Somme and Passchendaele. On Vimy Ridge, where your national memorial keeps watch, a corner of Europe will remain forever Canadian.

A generation later, in 1944, your boys came to our aid again, storming Normandy beaches alongside British and Americans to help liberate Europe from fascism. On that day, Canadian forces pushed farther inland than any other and, in some of the bloodiest fighting of the war, sustained heavy losses but soldiered on.
This sums up so much about the courageous Canadian spirit, and Europe will always be grateful for the sacrifice of so many who stood with us and defended freedom and democracy. We will never forget.
(Applause)

It is with that spirit, and with the weight of that history, that we now look to the future together. Yesterday's announcement – opening the door to deepening our alliance – is a huge positive step forward, with potential for closer collaboration on the issues that matter to people, to families and to industry on both sides of the Atlantic. The potential exists for better cooperation on so many different levels – from defence and trade to energy, education and research. Together we can break new and exciting ground, and ultimately improve lives.

Today is another milestone in that shared journey and your presence here, dear Mark, could not be more significant. I know we are all looking forward to hearing you speak. Thank you for being here. Without further ado, the floor is yours, Prime Minister.

interventions.speaker_label: Mark Carney, Premier Ministre du Canada.

paragraphs.text: Madame la Présidente Metsola, chère Roberta, Madame la Présidente von der Leyen, chère Ursula, membres honorables du Parlement européen, collègues distingués, je vous remercie de m'accorder l'honneur de prendre la parole devant vous en ce début de session décisive. Je vous parlerai aujourd'hui de la manière dont notre réponse à la rupture géopolitique actuelle devrait intégrer une nouvelle dimension.

Mais tout d'abord, j'aimerais évoquer un élément plus ancien, quelque chose qui remonte à bien avant les relations entre l'Union européenne et le Canada. Car la profondeur de nos liens ne se mesure pas avec des échanges commerciaux ni n'est inscrite dans nos traités. Nos liens sont profondément enracinés dans nos terres.

In the heart of Germany, above Weimar, there is a wooded ridge called Ettersberg. For decades, Goethe walked, thought and wrote there. An oak on that ridge came to bear his name – a living monument to the highest ideals of European culture. As the 20th century turned dark, that same oak became trapped behind the barbed wire of Buchenwald – a silent witness to humanity’s deepest moral failure.
Goethe understood that ideals must be fought for, that values do not defend themselves. Indeed, at the end of Faust, the old man’s last vision is of a free people on free ground.
„Nur der verdient sich Freiheit wie das Leben,
Der täglich sie erobern muß."
Freedom and life must be earned every single day.
(Applause)
Every day – not once in 1945 or 1956 or 1989, but every day, including this one.

La liberté a été conquise grâce à l'héroïsme de la résistance européenne pendant la guerre. Elle a été cultivée par les fondateurs de la Communauté européenne du charbon et de l'acier au lendemain de la guerre. Elle a été favorisée par la création de la Communauté européenne. Elle a été préservée par la mise en place de l'Union européenne et elle s'est développée grâce à son élargissement après la chute du mur de Berlin.
The values embodied by the Goethe oak have also endured, in part, because the ideals that flourished beneath its branches also crossed the Atlantic.

In 1917, amidst the devastation of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, a young Canadian Lieutenant named Leslie Miller gathered a handful of acorns from the shattered European landscape. He carried them home and planted them in Canadian soil in Milliken, Ontario, where they grew into a majestic forest. A century later, a profound circle of renewal was completed, because grafts from Leslie Miller’s Canadian oaks were repatriated to France and re-planted on the same Vimy Ridge where they had been born.
This is the essence of the Canada-European Union partnership: seeds, values, ideas, trade, people and progress carried back and forth across the Atlantic for centuries.
(Applause)

We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication. We hold common values, for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant. We believe that a strong economy is not an end in itself, but the means to a just society.
(Applause)
We are committed stewards of our natural heritage. We believe that our prosperity grows when it's shared. These values: this is a sharing of choice, not coincidence.
In his writings, Goethe borrowed a word from the chemists of his day: Wahlverwandtschaften, or the elective affinity of different elements that combine because of their inherent attraction.

Canada and Europe are not bound by geography, even though our Danish friends know that we share a 3 000 km border in the Arctic. We are bound by an affinity – elective, chosen, renewed, and stronger for being so.

Aujourd'hui, nos sociétés sont secouées par de nouvelles tempêtes: les bouleversements liés aux changements climatiques, l'érosion des normes démocratiques, l'utilisation du commerce comme arme. Les institutions multilatérales sur lesquelles nous comptions ont été affaiblies. La souveraineté et l'ouverture sont aujourd'hui difficiles à concilier. L'intégration économique est désormais utilisée comme une arme et les droits de douane comme un moyen de pression. Les mécanismes financiers ont été utilisés à des fins de coercition. Les chaînes d'approvisionnement constituent des points faibles à exploiter. Les technologies transforment la nature de la guerre, la structure des économies et la capacité des États à gouverner. Les plateformes technologiques aspirent à la souveraineté. Elles veulent fixer les conditions d'accès. Elles veulent dicter les règles en matière de réglementation et même les contourner. Elles veulent contrôler nos données, répandre la désinformation, voler l'enfance de nos enfants.
This combination is a ferocious storm: a single tree will come down in it; a forest will not.
(Applause)

That's because, beneath the forest floor, the roots of an oak intertwine with those of its neighbours – exchanging nutrients, adding strength to strength, creating a resilient, self-sustaining ecosystem. Together, Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values, while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive.

This is about sovereignty – our ability to live as we wish. It's about the freedoms we must fight for every day. Because sovereignty requires resilience, the ability to withstand shocks. Sovereignty today goes beyond being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves. It now requires secure access to AI, semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technologies, vaccines, space-based communications.

We all have important gaps in these strategic capabilities, and we each must rely on individual nations or individual companies to fill them. That creates vulnerabilities, particularly when supposedly global companies prove national in the breach. Closing these gaps is not possible alone, but it's very achievable collectively. Canada and Europe are each strong; Europe and Canada are stronger together.
(Applause)
The institutions we've inherited are organised by geography. The strategic capabilities that we need are organised by function. We can ally by function if we are bold and deliberate.

We shouldn't be cowed by the perceived scale of the task. Just as dominance is the arrogance of the hegemon, perfection is the enemy of the good. The economics of this are clear. The leverage of the powerful in an exploitative relationship collapses well before complete independence is achieved, because diversity confers advantage. The objective is not self-sufficiency; it's collective resilience.

It's this mutual advantage that's at the core of the case for a deeper partnership between Canada and Europe. Europe brings so many things: market power, research depth, advanced manufacturing, the ability and the will to set standards that the world frequently adopts, a defence industrial base that's being rebuilt at speed.

Canada brings energy at huge scale and in every form that the transition requires. We have one of the world's largest endowments of critical minerals, deep capabilities in space, AI and quantum, among the strongest banking systems and the most expert pension capital. We have unique Arctic geography, and privileged access to both Atlantic and Pacific networks.

Where our strengths differ, they complement. Where they overlap, they create scale. We should build on each other's strengths – deliberately, systematically and rapidly. We've already begun – and I thank this Parliament – with CETA, one of the world's most successful trade agreements. Thank you.
(Applause)

I thank President von der Leyen and President Costa for our strategic partnership agreement struck last June. We're developing and deepening it. We've also begun to take advantage of Canada's role as the first non-European member of SAFE. But we should recognise that the ecosystem we've built is not yet equal to the ferocity of the changing climate, nor is it moving fast enough to match the speed of the upheaval.
Yesterday, President von der Leyen spoke of moving beyond CETA to an alliance for the future, opening the door to Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member.
(Applause)

Canada welcomes this ambition, and I will tell you that polling shows that an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties with Europe. An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on our shared values.

But let me take this opportunity to say plainly what Canada proposes: Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities – including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments. We should move towards seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services.

We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to work, study and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic. Canadian membership of Erasmus+ would give your students and ours more opportunity to learn at some of the world's top universities, to broaden their horizons and to build those lasting ties that will sustain our alliance for the future.
Canadian membership of the next generation of Horizon would allow us to pool resources, cooperate on frontier technologies, and leverage our world-class research institutes and universities.
(Applause)

Yesterday, President von der Leyen announced, and I quote, a 'new European corporation on critical raw materials' to obtain and stockpile 'the material needed for electric cars, chips and batteries, clean tech, and defence'. I'll observe that Canada has deposits of over 34 critical minerals and we are among the top producers of the 10 most essential for the energy transition. Our alliance can help fill Europe's need for reliable supply, Canada's desire for advanced processing capabilities, and our common objective to complete value chains in the transition and our defence.

Canada can contribute LNG and hydrogen at large scale to support Europe's energy security, including by developing and leveraging new port infrastructure in our high north and on our east coast. Canada, in turn, can benefit from your leadership in so many clean energy technologies.

We can pool new sovereign compute capacity and build more secure broadband connections between Europe and Asia via our common geography. Canada and Europe can join forces to develop AI safety protocols, coordinate common standards and strengthen transparency, all while developing applications so that our governments and our companies can serve our citizens better. Canada and Europe should consider exploring an integrated market for financial services, to broaden choice and reduce cost for our citizens, to improve access to capital for our companies while maintaining our world-leading financial resilience.

These are some of the opportunities. But the fundamental point is that the opportunities that can be created by an alliance for the future are the product of our common values, our compatible systems and our complementary strengths. Deepening and widening our relationship will strengthen our sovereignty and improve affordability, opportunity and security for our citizens, while safeguarding our abilities to live our lives as we choose.
I also want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I'm not proposing a third block in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners.
(Applause)

We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.
(Applause)

These fundamental motivations, combined with our latent hard power, mean that we can help to create the next just, stable and prosperous world order. A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies, an alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability. An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens, and our citizens to do for themselves. An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices. An alliance open enough that others can join. An alliance principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than seeking to replace it.
(Applause)

To conclude, in my country, it's often said that Canada became a nation during the Battle of Vimy Ridge. And certainly, the thousands of Canadians who didn't return from that battle sacrificed their lives for something much bigger than themselves. One who did come home stopped first to pick up some acorns. And today, the same Vimy Oaks grow in Canada as in France: living proof that what we cultivate together can survive the darkest winter to thrive again.
So let us now deepen those roots, widen this canopy and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground every single day. Thank you very much.

We are committed stewards of our natural heritage. We believe that our prosperity grows when it's shared. These values: this is a sharing of choice, not coincidence.

In his writings, Goethe borrowed a word from the chemists of his day: Wahlverwandtschaften, or the elective affinity of different elements that combine because of their inherent attraction.

Canada and Europe are not bound by geography, even though our Danish friends know that we share a 3 000 km border in the Arctic. We are bound by an affinity – elective, chosen, renewed, and stronger for being so.

Aujourd'hui, nos sociétés sont secouées par de nouvelles tempêtes: les bouleversements liés aux changements climatiques, l'érosion des normes démocratiques, l'utilisation du commerce comme arme. Les institutions multilatérales sur lesquelles nous comptions ont été affaiblies. La souveraineté et l'ouverture sont aujourd'hui difficiles à concilier. L'intégration économique est désormais utilisée comme une arme et les droits de douane comme un moyen de pression. Les mécanismes financiers ont été utilisés à des fins de coercition. Les chaînes d'approvisionnement constituent des points faibles à exploiter. Les technologies transforment la nature de la guerre, la structure des économies et la capacité des États à gouverner. Les plateformes technologiques aspirent à la souveraineté. Elles veulent fixer les conditions d'accès. Elles veulent dicter les règles en matière de réglementation et même les contourner. Elles veulent contrôler nos données, répandre la désinformation, voler l'enfance de nos enfants.

This combination is a ferocious storm: a single tree will come down in it; a forest will not.

(Applause)

That's because, beneath the forest floor, the roots of an oak intertwine with those of its neighbours – exchanging nutrients, adding strength to strength, creating a resilient, self-sustaining ecosystem. Together, Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values, while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive.

This is about sovereignty – our ability to live as we wish. It's about the freedoms we must fight for every day. Because sovereignty requires resilience, the ability to withstand shocks. Sovereignty today goes beyond being able to feed, fuel and defend ourselves. It now requires secure access to AI, semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technologies, vaccines, space-based communications.

We all have important gaps in these strategic capabilities, and we each must rely on individual nations or individual companies to fill them. That creates vulnerabilities, particularly when supposedly global companies prove national in the breach. Closing these gaps is not possible alone, but it's very achievable collectively. Canada and Europe are each strong; Europe and Canada are stronger together.

(Applause)

The institutions we've inherited are organised by geography. The strategic capabilities that we need are organised by function. We can ally by function if we are bold and deliberate.

We shouldn't be cowed by the perceived scale of the task. Just as dominance is the arrogance of the hegemon, perfection is the enemy of the good. The economics of this are clear. The leverage of the powerful in an exploitative relationship collapses well before complete independence is achieved, because diversity confers advantage. The objective is not self-sufficiency; it's collective resilience.

It's this mutual advantage that's at the core of the case for a deeper partnership between Canada and Europe. Europe brings so many things: market power, research depth, advanced manufacturing, the ability and the will to set standards that the world frequently adopts, a defence industrial base that's being rebuilt at speed.

Canada brings energy at huge scale and in every form that the transition requires. We have one of the world's largest endowments of critical minerals, deep capabilities in space, AI and quantum, among the strongest banking systems and the most expert pension capital. We have unique Arctic geography, and privileged access to both Atlantic and Pacific networks.

Where our strengths differ, they complement. Where they overlap, they create scale. We should build on each other's strengths – deliberately, systematically and rapidly. We've already begun – and I thank this Parliament – with CETA, one of the world's most successful trade agreements. Thank you.

(Applause)

I thank President von der Leyen and President Costa for our strategic partnership agreement struck last June. We're developing and deepening it. We've also begun to take advantage of Canada's role as the first non-European member of SAFE. But we should recognise that the ecosystem we've built is not yet equal to the ferocity of the changing climate, nor is it moving fast enough to match the speed of the upheaval.

Yesterday, President von der Leyen spoke of moving beyond CETA to an alliance for the future, opening the door to Canada becoming the European Union's first associate member.

(Applause)

Canada welcomes this ambition, and I will tell you that polling shows that an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties with Europe. An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on our shared values.

But let me take this opportunity to say plainly what Canada proposes: Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities – including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments. We should move towards seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services.

We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to work, study and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic. Canadian membership of Erasmus+ would give your students and ours more opportunity to learn at some of the world's top universities, to broaden their horizons and to build those lasting ties that will sustain our alliance for the future.

Canadian membership of the next generation of Horizon would allow us to pool resources, cooperate on frontier technologies, and leverage our world-class research institutes and universities.

(Applause)

Yesterday, President von der Leyen announced, and I quote, a 'new European corporation on critical raw materials' to obtain and stockpile 'the material needed for electric cars, chips and batteries, clean tech, and defence'. I'll observe that Canada has deposits of over 34 critical minerals and we are among the top producers of the 10 most essential for the energy transition. Our alliance can help fill Europe's need for reliable supply, Canada's desire for advanced processing capabilities, and our common objective to complete value chains in the transition and our defence.

Canada can contribute LNG and hydrogen at large scale to support Europe's energy security, including by developing and leveraging new port infrastructure in our high north and on our east coast. Canada, in turn, can benefit from your leadership in so many clean energy technologies.

We can pool new sovereign compute capacity and build more secure broadband connections between Europe and Asia via our common geography. Canada and Europe can join forces to develop AI safety protocols, coordinate common standards and strengthen transparency, all while developing applications so that our governments and our companies can serve our citizens better. Canada and Europe should consider exploring an integrated market for financial services, to broaden choice and reduce cost for our citizens, to improve access to capital for our companies while maintaining our world-leading financial resilience.

These are some of the opportunities. But the fundamental point is that the opportunities that can be created by an alliance for the future are the product of our common values, our compatible systems and our complementary strengths. Deepening and widening our relationship will strengthen our sovereignty and improve affordability, opportunity and security for our citizens, while safeguarding our abilities to live our lives as we choose.

I also want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I'm not proposing a third block in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners.

(Applause)

We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.

(Applause)

These fundamental motivations, combined with our latent hard power, mean that we can help to create the next just, stable and prosperous world order. A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies, an alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability. An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens, and our citizens to do for themselves. An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices. An alliance open enough that others can join. An alliance principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than seeking to replace it.

(Applause)

To conclude, in my country, it's often said that Canada became a nation during the Battle of Vimy Ridge. And certainly, the thousands of Canadians who didn't return from that battle sacrificed their lives for something much bigger than themselves. One who did come home stopped first to pick up some acorns. And today, the same Vimy Oaks grow in Canada as in France: living proof that what we cultivate together can survive the darkest winter to thrive again.

So let us now deepen those roots, widen this canopy and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground every single day. Thank you very much.

interventions.text:
Señora presidenta, señorías, lamentamos que en España a los médicos hospitalarios se les exija de forma habitual trabajar en turnos de 24 horas sin parar, a veces de forma consecutiva y sin que se les garanticen los descansos compensatorios.

paragraphs.text: Signora Presidente, voglio innanzitutto ringraziare i relatori ombra e tutti coloro che hanno lavorato a questa relazione. In questi mesi è maturata tra noi una consapevolezza: siamo di fronte a una questione epocale che riguarda il rapporto tra i giovani e il mondo digitale. C'è il tema della dipendenza, della compulsività, del danno alla salute e dobbiamo intervenire subito.
Lo ha fatto la Presidente von der Leyen, prima riunendo gli esperti e ieri annunciando in quest'Aula un'iniziativa legislativa europea.

La nostra relazione ha colto il cambio di paradigma: la responsabilità principale è delle piattaforme, che devono rendere il mondo digitale sicuro e abitabile per i nostri ragazzi. Noi dobbiamo decidere e assumerci le nostre responsabilità.

Ma quando parliamo di dipendenza, salute e sviluppo dei giovani, dobbiamo prima ascoltare gli esperti. E gli esperti si sono pronunciati. La Presidente von der Leyen ha indicato una progressività nell'accesso dei minori: sotto i 13 anni niente social, dai 13 ai 15 anni accompagnati dai genitori e con limiti precisi.

Ora dobbiamo andare avanti e dobbiamo guardare anche alle decisioni prese negli Stati Uniti. Lì le piattaforme sono state chiamate a rispondere non soltanto economicamente ma anche con misure concrete. Quelle misure devono diventare regole europee.

Noi, alla legge del più forte nel mondo digitale, preferiamo la forza delle regole e il rispetto dei diritti, soprattutto di chi non ha ancora raggiunto la maggiore età. Se fissiamo un limite di età, dobbiamo avere anche uno strumento sicuro per verificarlo. E questo strumento esiste: è la soluzione europea per la verifica dell'età, il digital wallet, che crea regole comuni europee attuate poi a livello nazionale, che deve dire soltanto una cosa, se l'utente ha superato o meno la soglia di età richiesta.

Bisogna proteggere i minori e la loro privacy e, su questo punto, come Parlamento chiederemo le garanzie. Dunque divieti ma anche educazione digitale. L'Europa è sempre stata la culla del diritto deve esserla anche nel mondo digitale.

interventions.text: – Before the vote:

paragraphs.text: Senhora Presidente, não podemos pedir cada vez mais aos nossos pescadores e oferecer‑lhes cada vez menos para continuarem a pescar. É esta a principal mensagem deste relatório.

Quero falar de quem está no mar, de quem de madrugada enfrenta o mau tempo e coloca a vida em risco, os custos de combustível, a burocracia e a incerteza, mas, apesar de tudo isso, continua a garantir alimento às nossas famílias.

Os pescadores europeus cumprem inúmeras regras ambientais, sanitárias, de segurança, de controlo, de rastreabilidade, de combate à pesca ilegal. E, na União Europeia, defendemos oceanos saudáveis e uma pesca sustentável. Mas sustentabilidade também significa ter rendimento para viver, barcos seguros para trabalhar, e jovens que queiram continuar esta profissão. Não podemos impor estas e outras obrigações aos pescadores europeus enquanto entram no nosso mercado produtos provenientes de países onde estas mesmas exigências não existem ou não são equivalentes.

Recordo que hoje importamos mais de 80 % dos produtos de pesca e de aquacultura que consumimos na União Europeia. A reciprocidade é uma exigência. Quem quer vender no mercado europeu deve respeitar as nossas regras. E, para os nossos, precisamos de menos burocracia, mais investimentos, uma frota mais moderna e segura, apoiar particularmente a pequena pesca, as comunidades costeiras, as nossas ilhas e as regiões ultraperiféricas, e garantir que um jovem que hoje olhe para o nosso mar possa sentir que a pesca é o seu futuro.

Os pescadores são parte da solução para a segurança alimentar, para a nossa economia e para a proteção dos nossos oceanos. Queremos pescadores no mar, peixe europeu nas nossas mesas e comunidades costeiras com futuro. É por isso que defendemos uma pesca sustentável, sim, mas também economicamente viável, socialmente justa e com condições de concorrência leal. Por isso, é fundamental revermos a política comum de pescas com um verdadeiro pacote de simplificação, com um financiamento europeu específico e protegido no próximo quadro financeiro plurianual, e restabelecer o POSEI Pescas para as nossas regiões ultraperiféricas.
Proteger o mar é essencial. Proteger quem vive no mar também é.

paragraphs.text: The next item is the Commission statement on protecting people's health against toxic substances (2026/2877(RSP)).

Although this is the last debate in this week's parliament session, it is a very important debate which reflects on the health of the EU citizens and toxic substances which are endangering our health. We have had recent examples from all across Europe of PFAS-containing hazardous waste – Italy, Slovenia, Germany, the city of Gospić in Croatia. As the Chair of this sitting, I want to express my full solidarity with the citizens and the willingness of the EU to protect the interests of our citizens.

Although this is the last debate in this week's parliament session, it is a very important debate which reflects on the health of the EU citizens and toxic substances which are endangering our health. We have had recent examples from all across Europe of PFAS-containing hazardous waste – Italy, Slovenia, Germany, the city of Gospić in Croatia. As the Chair of this sitting, I want to express my full solidarity with the citizens and the willingness of the EU to protect the interests of our citizens.

interventions.speaker_label: Olivér Várhelyi, Member of the Commission.

paragraphs.text: Mr President, honourable Members, protecting health is a foundation for us, as citizens, and for our economy as well. It is also not one-dimensional. It spans from every level of governance to various policy fields.

So let me start with one risk factor that is both the most harmful and the easiest to avoid, which is tobacco. Tobacco-related mortality in the EU fell from approximately 700 000 people in 2012 to about 530 000 in 2023. This is very important progress, but this means that over half a million people in the EU still die every year as a result of tobacco use.

New nicotine products are spreading, especially in younger generations. More than half of nicotine pouch users are under 40. One in five consumers of tobacco and nicotine products aged between 15 to 19 years of age started by regularly using already e-cigarettes.

In fact, we need to address e-cigarettes with nicotine or without. The aerosol they produce can contain toxic metals such as lead, nickel, and chromium, along with other harmful chemicals. These substances cause documented damage to the nervous, cardiovascular, and also the respiratory systems. Our rules, therefore, need to keep pace with the rapidly changing market.

That is why we are working on the update of the tobacco legislation to provide more effective protection against those products, as promised under the Safe Hearts Plan. In it, we will also address the increasingly aggressive digital marketing that is making these products more attractive, especially to those younger audiences. So the Commission is now carrying out an impact assessment, drawing on a broad consultation process.

Second, protecting people's health starts with the people that care for patients. This is one reason why we phased out the use of dental amalgam in the EU from the beginning of 2025, significantly reducing exposure to mercury. Together with your help, the latest update to the carcinogens, mutagens and reprotoxic substances directive was just finalised and, to better protect workers, it will tackle specific substances with maximum exposure limits.

Protection cannot stop at the workplace. A healthy environment underpins people's health. Against this backdrop, the Commission significantly updated its environmental rules during the last mandate, tightening air and water pollution rules, industrial emissions standards and waste management. The Commission also continued its work under the EU chemicals legislation, REACH, addressing various hazardous substances. Currently, ECHA is in the final phase of assessing the general PFAS restriction.

Finally, let me turn to something that concerns every European, every day: the food on our table. Food in Europe must be safe. EU law protects human health from risks related to contaminants and plant protection residues in food. Maximum levels of contaminants and plant protection residues in food are set out in legislation following risk assessments by the European Food Safety Authority.

Strong limits require proper enforcement and monitoring. During the last three years of monitoring, 98.8 % of samples were free of residues or were within the legal limits. Member States enforce our laws, for example by withdrawing non-compliant products from the market.

The same principle applies to food imports. Import controls make sure that non-compliant products are rejected at the border and do not enter our markets. To strengthen the EU's import control system, earlier this year the Commission launched a new task force on import controls, coupled with immediate practical measures. These measures include increasing audits in non-EU countries by 50 % and audits at EU border control points by 33 %.

We have created a pool of 30 national experts, and their visits to the border control posts have started this week on 14 September. Additionally, around 650 national officials will receive dedicated EU training. The task force will better target controls, audits and monitoring where they can have the greatest impact.

So honourable Members, whether the risk comes from tobacco and nicotine products, exposure at work, chemicals in our environment or contaminants in our food, Europeans expect us to protect their health. I look forward to hearing about your perspectives.

paragraphs.text: Poštovani predsjedavajući, povjereniče, kolegice i kolege, zaštita zdravlja ljudi nije ni lijeva, ali nije ni desna tema.

Čista voda, zrak i okoliš se tiču sviju nas. I zato kada dođe do problema, kada dođe do propusta ili kada dođe do ovakvih situacija, s kakvim se, nažalost suočavamo i u Hrvatskoj, ozbiljna politika rješava problem, a ne širi strah i paniku. Ozbiljna politika građanima donosi rezultate sanacije, a ne koristi strah građana za svoje planove.

Nezakonito gospodarenje otpadom predstavlja zajednički europski izazov koji se tiče baš svake države članice jer je i ekološki kriminal često prekograničnog karaktera, a kao što znamo, i jedna od najunosnijih aktivnosti organiziranog kriminala. Nezakonito odlaganje više od 35 tisuća tona opasnog otpada u Varaždinu, u Gospiću i u Benkovcu koje je otkriveno uz pomoć Europola, pokazuje koliko šteta može nastati takvim nezakonitim djelovanjem. Ali zato je još jasnije da briga za zdravlje se ne može i ne dokazuje se glasnoćom ideološkog napada, nego neovisnim analizama, javnim podacima i rokovima sanacije. Ovaj slučaj zbog toga nije još jedna prilika za ideološko nadmetanje, nego test snage naše pravne države. Građani imaju pravo na istinu, na kontinuirani zdravstveni nadzor i za sanaciju s jasnim rokovima, a počinitelji bez ikakve dileme moraju biti procesuirani i odgovarati.

Zaključno, kolegice i kolege, jasno je da nećemo birati između ignoriranja problema s jedne strane i širenja panike s druge strane, nego da biramo mjerenje, transparentnost, sanaciju i odgovornost, konkretne mjere koje će predstaviti kolege iz Delegacije, biramo zaštititi svoje sugrađane, a ne napuniti ih strahom i onda na tom strahu politički jahati.

interventions.speaker_label: Romana Jerković, u ime kluba S&D.

paragraphs.text: Poštovani predsjedavajući, kolegice i kolege, povjereniče, prije svega željela bih reći da postavljati pitanja nije širenje panike, već zaštita građana.

Koliko je važna današnja rasprava ilustrirat ću na primjeru grada Gospića, u mojoj Hrvatskoj. Grad Gospić danas ima oko 35 tisuća tona ilegalno odloženog otpada, više od tri tone po svakom stanovniku. Takva ekološka katastrofa ne nastaje preko noći. Ona nastaje kada vlast godinama zatvara oči i kada pogoduje interesima dobro povezanih pojedinaca umjesto da štiti građane. Ona nastaje kada korupcija, pogodovanje i politička šutnja postanu važniji od zdravlja građana.

Neki sada pokušavaju prebaciti krivnju isključivo na prekogranični promet otpada i međunarodni kriminal. Da, to bez sumnje treba istražiti, ali pravila postoje i ona su vrlo jasna. Pitanje je zašto ih Vlada i državne institucije nisu provodile. Kako je moguće da su tisuće kamiona s opasnim otpadom iz nekoliko država prešle granicu, a da ih nitko nije pregledao? Kako je moguće da su završile zakopane u Gospiću? Kako je moguće da i nakon nekoliko desetaka inspekcijskih nadzora, država nije uspjela spriječiti razmjere ilegalnog odlaganja i to ne samo u Gospiću, već i na drugim lokacijama? Samo u slučaju Gospića prekršen je Ugovor o funkcioniranju Europske unije, barem pet europskih direktiva i zakona te dvije konvencije povezane s otpadom.

I još nešto, zakonski rok za zbrinjavanje nezakonito unesenog otpada je 30 dana, a što mi danas u Gospiću imamo nakon 580 dana od uhićenja? Ovo je samo jedan primjer od mnogih, kao da zaštita zdravlja ljudi od otrovnih i opasnih tvari su pitanje političke volje. E nisu. To je obveza države i njenih institucija, a kada država zakaže, onda se moramo obratiti europskim institucijama.
To je posljednja linija obrane zdravlja naših građana na koju ovaj puta ozbiljno računamo.

political_group.label: S&D
political_group.name: Group of the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats in the European Parliament

interventions.speaker_label: Mélanie Disdier, au nom du groupe PfE.

paragraphs.text: Monsieur le Président, protéger la santé de nos concitoyens face aux substances toxiques est une exigence absolue. C'est un défi qui réclame de la rigueur, de l'exigence et surtout de la rationalité. Or, dans cet hémicycle, et particulièrement sur les bancs de la gauche et des Verts, la rationalité scientifique a depuis bien longtemps cédé sa place à la panique morale et à l'idéologie.

Rappelons une évidence connue depuis longtemps: c'est la dose qui fait le poison. Aujourd'hui, la technologie nous permet de détecter des traces de substances à une échelle infime, c'est-à-dire un milliardième de milligramme. Mais détecter une molécule ne signifie pas que le seuil de toxicité est atteint. Pourtant, l'extrême gauche et les écologistes entretiennent sciemment cette confusion. Ils confondent systématiquement la présence d'une trace avec un risque sanitaire avéré. Et cette politique de la peur a des conséquences concrètes. Cette politique de la peur a des conséquences désastreuses. En toxicologie, cela porte un nom: la substitution regrettable.

Sous la pression d'un discours alarmiste et déconnecté du réel, vous, la gauche, les macronistes, exigez des interdictions brutales sans aucune alternative viable. Quel en est le résultat? Regardons, par exemple, l'agriculture. En interdisant bêtement les néonicotinoïdes, vous forcez nos cultivateurs, notamment dans la filière de la betterave, à pulvériser davantage en amont avec des insecticides, en les obligeant à multiplier les passages de tracteur.

Au nom d'une prétendue protection, vous avez aggravé le problème. Vous ne faites pas de l'écologie, vous faites de l'idéologie. Mais au-delà de ces conséquences agricoles, la plus grande supercherie de votre politique européenne réside dans le cynisme commercial. Vous imposez à nos agriculteurs et à nos industriels les normes les plus drastiques du monde. J'en profite d'ailleurs pour saluer l'immense qualité de l'agriculture française, la plus vertueuse au monde.

Mais en même temps, la Commission européenne laisse nos frontières grandes ouvertes à des produits étrangers traités avec des phytos que nous, nous n'avons même pas et que nous avons strictement interdits sur notre sol. Où est la protection de la santé humaine, quand l'Union européenne importe massivement des denrées agricoles traitées avec des phytos interdits chez nous, tout en pénalisant nos propres producteurs? L'absence de véritable clause miroir est une trahison sanitaire autant qu'une injustice économique.

Au Rassemblement national, nous portons une autre vision. Nous croyons en la science et au progrès, pas en l'obscurantisme des Verts. La protection de la santé humaine ne passera pas par une asphyxie réglementaire, mais par la souveraineté en protégeant nos frontières, en finançant la recherche pour trouver des alternatives réelles et en cessant de transformer la noble cause de la santé publique en un outil de décroissance punitive.
